goals: Recall the surface-area formulas of the six basic solids
Find the slant height of a cone
Decide which faces are visible when two solids are joined
Find the surface area of combinations of two solids in real objects
Handle solids with a part scooped out

slides.narration: Welcome to Surface Areas and Volumes. Look at a kulfi: it is a cone topped with a hemisphere. A tent is a cylinder with a cone on top, and a gas cylinder is a cylinder with two hemispheres. In this part we find the surface area of such combined solids. The one new idea is to count only the faces you can see.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Use the surface-area formulas for **cuboid, cube, cylinder, cone, sphere, hemisphere**
Spot the **hidden faces** when solids are joined
Find surface areas of tents, kulfis, toys and tanks
Handle a hemisphere **scooped out** of a solid
slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. You met these six solids in class nine. This year the syllabus combines any two of them, as in real objects. Note that converting one solid into another, and the frustum of a cone, are not in the syllabus this year.

slides.heading: The six basic solids
slides.body_md: Every combined solid in this chapter is made of two of these.

visual.alt: Formula table for six solids: cuboid, cube, cylinder, cone, sphere and hemisphere, giving the curved or lateral surface area, the total surface area and the volume of each.
visual.caption: Learn this table: every combined solid is built from it.

slides.narration: Here is the formula table for the six solids. For each one, know the curved surface, the total surface and the volume. Notice the hemisphere: its curved surface is two pi r squared, half a sphere, and its total surface adds the flat circle, three pi r squared. That difference matters a lot in combined solids.

slides.heading: The slant height of a cone
slides.body_md: The radius $r$, height $h$ and slant height $l$ form a right triangle:

visual.alt: A right circular cone with base radius r, vertical height h from the centre of the base to the apex, and slant height l along the side; r, h and l form a right triangle.
visual.caption: Slant height: $l = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$.

slides.narration: The curved surface of a cone uses the slant height l, not the vertical height h. The radius, the height and the slant height form a right triangle, with l as the hypotenuse. So l is the square root of r squared plus h squared. Use h for volume and l for surface area. Mixing them up is the most common mistake in this chapter.

slides.heading: Quick check: curved surface of a cone
slides.body_md: Which length goes into $\pi rl$?
slides.narration: The curved surface needs the slant height. Is it given, or do you need Pythagoras first?

slides.heading: Joining solids hides faces
slides.body_md: When two solids are joined, the faces in contact go **inside**. The surface area of the combination is the sum of the **visible** surfaces only.
bullets: Cone on a cylinder: the top of the cylinder and the base of the cone are hidden
Hemisphere on a cone: use the hemisphere's **curved** surface $2\pi r^2$
So: TSA of a combination $\ne$ sum of TSAs

visual.alt: Table of combined solids: a tent loses the joining circle and the floor; a kulfi loses the joining circle; a capsule loses both end circles; a cube with a hemispherical hollow loses a circle from one face but gains the bowl.
visual.caption: Add the surfaces you can touch from outside; drop the joined faces.

slides.narration: Imagine painting a combined solid. You can only paint what you can touch from outside. Where two solids are glued, the faces in contact disappear inside. So never add total surface areas blindly. List the visible pieces: usually curved surfaces, plus any flat face that is still outside, such as the bottom of a rocket.

slides.narration: A tent has no floor, and inside it there is no wall where the cone meets the cylinder. So the canvas is just the two curved surfaces. Find the slant height first: three point seven metres. Then take pi r out as a common factor: eleven times nine point seven gives one hundred and six point seven square metres.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: wrapping a kulfi
slides.body_md: A kulfi is a cone of radius $3.5$ cm and height $12$ cm with a hemisphere of radius $3.5$ cm on top. Find the area of foil that covers it completely. (Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.)
bullets: **Step 2 —** Visible: curved cone $\pi rl$ and curved hemisphere $2\pi r^2$.
**Trap —** $3\pi r^2$ would wrongly add the hidden flat circle.

slides.narration: The flat face of the hemisphere is glued to the base of the cone, so neither is outside. That leaves two curved surfaces. Taking pi r common keeps the arithmetic short: eleven times nineteen point five, two hundred and fourteen point five square centimetres. If you wrote three pi r squared for the hemisphere, you counted a hidden circle.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a hemisphere scooped out
slides.body_md: A hemisphere of radius $3$ cm is scooped out of the top face of a wooden cube of edge $10$ cm. Find the total surface area of the remaining solid. (Use $\pi = 3.14$.)
bullets: **Step 2 —** The top face loses a circle: $-\pi r^2$. The hollow adds a bowl: $+2\pi r^2$.

slides.narration: Scooping makes the surface bigger, which surprises many students. A circle disappears from the top face, but the inside of the bowl becomes new surface, and the bowl is twice the circle. So the net change is plus one pi r squared, twenty eight point two six square centimetres, giving six hundred and twenty eight point two six.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: an oil tanker
slides.body_md: The body of an oil tanker is a cylinder $7$ m long and of radius $1.4$ m, with a hemisphere at each end. Find the area to be painted and the cost at ₹$120$ per m². (Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.)
bullets: **Step 2 —** Two hemispheres $=$ one sphere: $4\pi r^2 = 4 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 1.96 = 24.64$ m².

slides.narration: Both flat ends of the cylinder are covered by hemispheres, so they vanish. What remains is the curved surface of the cylinder and two curved hemispheres, which together make a whole sphere. Add them: eighty six point two four square metres. Multiply by the rate for the cost. Always check that the rate and the area use the same unit.

slides.heading: Planning a surface-area answer
slides.body_md: Write the plan in one line before calculating: it earns a mark and avoids hidden faces.

visual.alt: Flow for surface area of a combined solid: split it into basic solids, cross out the joined faces, add the visible surfaces, and answer in square units.
visual.caption: Surface area: visible faces only.

slides.narration: Here is a four-step plan. Split the object into basic solids. Cross out every face that is joined, and any face that is open, like the floor of a tent. Add the visible surfaces, taking common factors such as pi r. Finally write the unit, square metres or square centimetres.

slides.narration: When you scoop out a bowl, which flat area is lost and which curved area appears? Compare them.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Six basic solids — learn their CSA, TSA and volume
$l = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$; use $l$ for surface, $h$ for volume
Hemisphere glued on: $2\pi r^2$; two hemispheres $= 4\pi r^2$

rows: no lid, no floor: leave those faces out

visual.alt: Summary table of part one: slant height is the square root of r squared plus h squared; joined faces are never counted; a hemisphere on a solid uses its curved surface 2 pi r squared; scooping a hemisphere removes pi r squared and adds 2 pi r squared; open objects have no lid or floor.
visual.caption: Surface area rules.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. Start from the six basic formulas. Find the slant height when a cone is involved. For combined solids, count only the visible faces: glued faces and open faces are left out. And remember the surprising rule: scooping out a hemisphere increases the surface area by pi r squared.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Surface area (3 marks):** slant height 1 + correct visible faces 1 + answer with unit 1
**Mistake:** $3\pi r^2$ for a hemisphere that is glued on
**Mistake:** adding total surface areas of the parts
**Mistake:** cm² and m² mixed in one answer
slides.narration: Show the slant height on its own line; it earns a mark. Then write in words which surfaces you are adding, for example curved surface of cylinder plus curved surface of cone. That sentence shows the examiner you understood the combination. Keep units consistent, and give the final answer with the right square unit.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. A grain silo is a cylinder with a conical roof. How much grain fits inside? For volume the rule is even simpler than for surface area: joined solids add up, and parts that are cut out are subtracted. We will also convert cubic units into litres for capacity questions.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Use the **volume** formulas of the six solids
Solve silo, tank, toy and container problems
slides.narration: These are your goals. Unlike surface area, volume does not care about hidden faces: the space inside a combined solid is simply the space of its parts put together. The skill is to identify the parts correctly and to keep track of units.

slides.heading: Volume of a combined solid
slides.body_md: Joined solids: **add** the volumes. Cut-outs: **subtract**.

visual.alt: Flow for volume of a combined solid: split it into basic solids, add the volumes of parts that are joined, subtract the volumes of parts that are cut out, and answer in cubic units or litres.
visual.caption: Volume: add what is joined, subtract what is removed.

slides.narration: Here is the plan. Split the object into basic solids. If two parts are joined, add their volumes. If a part has been cut out, subtract its volume. Then write the answer in cubic units, or convert to litres if the question asks for capacity. That is the whole method.

sections.heading: 1. The six basic solids
sections.body_md:
| Solid | Curved / lateral surface | Total surface | Volume |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cuboid | $2h(l + b)$ | $2(lb + bh + hl)$ | $lbh$ |
| Cube | $4a^2$ | $6a^2$ | $a^3$ |
| Cylinder | $2\pi rh$ | $2\pi r(r + h)$ | $\pi r^2h$ |
| Cone | $\pi rl$ | $\pi r(l + r)$ | $\frac13\pi r^2h$ |
| Sphere | — | $4\pi r^2$ | $\frac43\pi r^3$ |
| Hemisphere | $2\pi r^2$ | $3\pi r^2$ | $\frac23\pi r^3$ |

Use the value of $\pi$ the question gives. *Not in the 2026–27 syllabus:* conversion of one solid into another (melting, recasting, digging) and the frustum of a cone.

sections.heading: 2. The cone and its slant height
sections.body_md:
For a cone of radius $r$ and vertical height $h$, the slant height is

$$l = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}.$$

Use $l$ in the curved surface $\pi rl$ and $h$ in the volume $\dfrac13\pi r^2h$. Useful triples: $(5, 12, 13)$, $(7, 24, 25)$, $(21, 20, 29)$, $(3.5, 12, 12.5)$, $(2.8, 2.1, 3.5)$.

A cone and a cylinder with the same base and height: the cone has one-third of the volume.

key_terms.definition_md: The distance from the apex of a cone to any point on the edge of its base.

sections.heading: 3. Surface area of a combination
sections.body_md:
**Rule:** add the **visible** surfaces only. Faces in contact are inside the solid; open faces (a tent's floor, a cup's top) are not there.

- Tent (cylinder $+$ cone, no floor): $2\pi rh + \pi rl$.
- Kulfi or toy (cone $+$ hemisphere): $\pi rl + 2\pi r^2$.
- Capsule or tanker (cylinder $+$ two hemispheres): $2\pi rh + 4\pi r^2$.
- Rocket (cylinder $+$ cone, with bottom): $2\pi rh + \pi r^2 + \pi rl$.
- Cube with a cube or cuboid on top: the covered square reappears as the top of the upper block, so add only its side faces.

Joining two solids with a common circle of radius $r$ removes $2\pi r^2$ from the sum of their total surfaces.

sections.heading: 4. Scooping out and sticking on
sections.body_md:
- **Scooping a hemisphere** of radius $r$ from a face: the face loses $\pi r^2$, the bowl adds $2\pi r^2$ — surface **increases** by $\pi r^2$; volume **decreases** by $\dfrac23\pi r^3$.
- **Sticking a hemisphere** on a face: the face loses $\pi r^2$ (covered), the dome adds $2\pi r^2$ — surface increases by $\pi r^2$; volume increases by $\dfrac23\pi r^3$.
- **Hollowing a cone** from a cylinder (same $r$, $h$): the top circle goes, the inside of the cone $\pi rl$ appears; volume left $= \dfrac23\pi r^2h$.

*Example:* cube of edge $10$ cm with a hemisphere of radius $3$ cm scooped out: surface $600 + 28.26 = 628.26$ cm².

sections.heading: 5. Volume of a combination
sections.body_md:
**Rule:** joined parts **add**; removed parts **subtract**.

- Cylinder $+$ cone on the same base: $\pi r^2\left(h_1 + \dfrac{h_2}{3}\right)$ (silo $r = 3.5$, $h_1 = 10$, $h_2 = 3$: $423.5$ m³).
- Cone $+$ hemisphere: $\dfrac13\pi r^2(h + 2r)$ (kulfi $r = 3.5$, $h = 12$: $\approx 243.83$ cm³).
- Cylinder $+$ hemisphere: $\pi r^2\left(h + \dfrac{2r}{3}\right)$.
- Block with a hollow: block $-$ hollow.

When the **total** height of a vessel with a hemispherical bottom is given, the cylinder's height is total $-$ $r$. The smallest box around a solid has the same radius and the full height.

sections.heading: 6. Units and capacity
sections.body_md:
- $1$ m³ $= 1000$ litres; $1$ litre $= 1000$ cm³ $= 1000$ mL; $1$ m³ $= 10^6$ cm³.
- Capacity is the volume of the inside of a container.
- Cost $=$ area $\times$ rate (per m² or per cm²) or volume $\times$ rate; keep units consistent.

*Example:* tank $74.844$ m³ $= 74844$ litres.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Surface area (2–3 marks):* slant height 1; visible faces named 1; answer with unit 1.
- *Volume (2–3 marks):* each part 1; sum or difference with unit 1.
- *Long questions (5 marks):* typically slant height, surface, cost, volume and a conversion, one mark each.

**Common mistakes**
1. Slant height in a volume, or vertical height in $\pi rl$.
2. $3\pi r^2$ for a hemisphere that is glued to another solid.
3. Adding total surface areas of the parts.
4. Forgetting $\dfrac13$ (cone) or $\dfrac23$ (hemisphere).
5. Using the total height as the cylinder's height.
6. Litres: multiply m³ by $1000$, divide cm³ by $1000$.

questions.stem_md: The curved surface area of a hemisphere of radius $r$ is
questions.solution_md: A hemisphere has half the surface of a sphere: $\dfrac12 \times 4\pi r^2 = 2\pi r^2$. Option (b) is its **total** surface area (curved surface $+$ flat circle $\pi r^2$).

questions.stem_md: The slant height of a cone with base radius $5$ cm and height $12$ cm is
questions.solution_md: $l = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2} = \sqrt{25 + 144} = \sqrt{169} = 13$ cm. Option (a) subtracts the squares.

questions.stem_md: The total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius $7$ cm is (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution_md: Total surface $=$ curved $2\pi r^2$ $+$ flat face $\pi r^2 = 3\pi r^2 = 3 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 49 = 462$ cm². Option (d) is the curved surface only; (a) is a whole sphere.

questions.stem_md: A solid is made by placing a hemisphere on top of a cylinder of the same radius. Its total surface area is

options.text_md: TSA of cylinder + TSA of hemisphere
CSA of cylinder + TSA of hemisphere
TSA of cylinder + CSA of hemisphere
CSA of cylinder + CSA of hemisphere + area of the bottom circle

questions.solution_md: The joining circle (top of the cylinder $=$ flat face of the hemisphere) is inside the solid and is not part of its surface. What remains: the cylinder's curved surface, its bottom circle, and the hemisphere's curved surface. Options (a)–(c) count a hidden circle at least once.

questions.stem_md: Three cubes, each of edge $3$ cm, are joined end to end in a row. The surface area of the resulting cuboid is
questions.solution_md: The cuboid is $9 \times 3 \times 3$: $2(27 + 9 + 27) = 126$ cm². Option (b) adds the three cubes' surfaces ($3 \times 54$), counting the four hidden faces.

questions.stem_md: The volume of a hemisphere of radius $21$ cm is (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution_md: $V = \dfrac23 \pi r^3 = \dfrac23 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 9261 = 19404$ cm³. Option (c) is the whole sphere; (a) is the curved surface area in cm².

questions.stem_md: A cone and a cylinder have the same base radius and the same height. The ratio of the volume of the cone to that of the cylinder is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{\frac13\pi r^2h}{\pi r^2h} = \dfrac13$.

questions.stem_md: A toy rocket is a cylinder of radius $7$ cm and height $10$ cm with a cone of the same radius and height $6$ cm on top. Its volume is (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution_md: Cylinder $= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 49 \times 10 = 1540$ cm³; cone $= \dfrac13 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 49 \times 6 = 308$ cm³. Total $= 1848$ cm³. Option (a) forgets the $\dfrac13$ in the cone.

questions.stem_md: The curved surface area of a cone of radius $7$ cm and slant height $25$ cm is (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution_md: $\pi rl = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 25 = 550$ cm². Option (b) is the total surface area ($550 + 154$).

questions.stem_md: A solid is a cylinder (radius $r$, height $h$) with a hemisphere of radius $r$ at each end. Its total surface area is
questions.solution_md: Both flat ends of the cylinder are covered by the hemispheres. Visible: the cylinder's curved surface $2\pi rh$ and two hemispherical curved surfaces $2 \times 2\pi r^2$. Option (d) wrongly keeps the cylinder's two end circles.

questions.stem_md: A hemisphere of radius $3.5$ cm is scooped out of a solid cube of edge $7$ cm. The volume of the remaining solid is about (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution_md: Cube $= 343$ cm³; hemisphere $= \dfrac23 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 42.875 \approx 89.83$ cm³. Remaining $= 343 - 89.83 = 253.17$ cm³. Option (d) adds instead of subtracting; (b) is the hemisphere alone.

questions.stem_md: An ice-cream cone is filled and topped with a hemisphere of ice cream of the same radius. The total outer surface of this shape is
questions.solution_md: The cone's base circle is the hemisphere's flat face: it is hidden. Visible: curved cone $\pi rl$ $+$ curved hemisphere $2\pi r^2$.

questions.stem_md: $1$ m³ is equal to
questions.solution_md: $1$ m³ $= 100 \times 100 \times 100$ cm³ $= 1000000$ cm³, and $1$ litre $= 1000$ cm³, so $1$ m³ $= 1000$ litres. Option (d) is the number of cm³.

questions.stem_md: A cylindrical tank has radius $0.7$ m and height $2$ m. Its capacity is (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution_md: $V = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 0.49 \times 2 = 3.08$ m³ $= 3.08 \times 1000 = 3080$ litres.

questions.stem_md: A cone is placed on top of a cylinder of the same radius $r$. Compared with the sum of the total surface areas of the two separate solids, the total surface area of the combined solid is
questions.solution_md: Joining hides **two** circles of area $\pi r^2$: the cylinder's top and the cone's base. So the combined surface is $2\pi r^2$ less than the sum.

questions.stem_md: A toy is a cone of radius $3$ cm and height $4$ cm on a hemisphere of radius $3$ cm. Its volume is (use $\pi = 3.14$)
questions.solution_md: Cone $= \dfrac13 \pi \times 9 \times 4 = 12\pi$; hemisphere $= \dfrac23 \pi \times 27 = 18\pi$. Total $= 30\pi = 30 \times 3.14 = 94.2$ cm³. Options (b) and (c) are the parts alone; (a) uses a whole sphere ($36\pi$).

questions.stem_md: The surface area of a sphere is $616$ cm². Its radius is (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution_md: $4 \times \dfrac{22}{7} r^2 = 616 \Rightarrow r^2 = 49 \Rightarrow r = 7$ cm. Option (c) stops at $r^2$.

questions.stem_md: A cone with the same base and height as a solid cylinder is carved out of it. The volume left is what fraction of the cylinder?
questions.solution_md: $\pi r^2h - \dfrac13\pi r^2h = \dfrac23\pi r^2h$: two-thirds of the cylinder.

**Reason (R):** A solid hemisphere has a curved surface of area $2\pi r^2$ and a flat circular face of area $\pi r^2$.

**Assertion (A):** The volume of a hemisphere of radius $3$ cm is $36\pi$ cm³.

**Reason (R):** The volume of a sphere of radius $r$ is $\dfrac43\pi r^3$.

**Assertion (A):** The volume of a toy made of a cone (radius $r$, height $h$) on a hemisphere of radius $r$ is $\dfrac13\pi r^2(h + 2r)$.

**Reason (R):** The volume of a solid made by joining two solids without overlap is the sum of their volumes.

**Reason (R):** The slant height of a cone of radius $r$ and height $h$ is $\sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$.

questions.stem_md: The volume of a hemisphere is half the volume of a sphere of the same radius.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac23\pi r^3 = \dfrac12 \times \dfrac43\pi r^3$.

questions.stem_md: The total surface area of two cubes joined face to face is the sum of the total surface areas of the two cubes.
questions.solution_md: The two faces that touch are hidden, so the joined solid has $2a^2$ less surface: $10a^2$ instead of $12a^2$.

questions.stem_md: The curved surface area of a cylinder of radius $r$ and height $h$ is $2\pi rh$.
questions.solution_md: Unrolled, the curved surface is a rectangle $2\pi r$ long and $h$ wide.

questions.stem_md: A cone of radius $7$ cm and height $24$ cm has a slant height of $31$ cm.
questions.solution_md: $l = \sqrt{49 + 576} = \sqrt{625} = 25$ cm. Adding $7 + 24$ is the mistake.

questions.stem_md: If a hemisphere of radius $r$ is scooped out of a face of a solid cube, the total surface area of the solid increases by $\pi r^2$.
questions.solution_md: A circle of area $\pi r^2$ is removed from the face, but the inside of the bowl, $2\pi r^2$, is added: net change $+\pi r^2$.

questions.stem_md: The slant height $l$ of a cone with radius $r$ and height $h$ is $l =$ ___.
questions.solution_md: $r$, $h$ and $l$ form a right triangle with hypotenuse $l$: $l = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$.

questions.stem_md: The volume of a cone is ___ of the volume of a cylinder with the same base and height.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac13\pi r^2h$ against $\pi r^2h$.

questions.stem_md: 1 litre = ___ cm³.
questions.solution_md: $1$ litre $= 1000$ cm³ (and $1000$ litres $= 1$ m³).

questions.stem_md: The curved surface area of a hemisphere of radius $7$ cm is ___ cm² (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$).
questions.solution_md: $2\pi r^2 = 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 49 = 308$ cm².

questions.stem_md: The volume of a sphere of radius $3$ cm is ___ $\pi$ cm³.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac43\pi \times 27 = 36\pi$ cm³.

questions.stem_md: Find the total surface area (in cm²) of a closed solid cylinder of radius $7$ cm and height $10$ cm. Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** TSA $= 2\pi r(r + h)$.

**Step 2.** $2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 \times (7 + 10) = 44 \times 17 = 748$ cm².

questions.stem_md: Find the curved surface area (in cm²) of a cone of radius $21$ cm and height $20$ cm. Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.
A wooden toy rocket is a cylinder of radius $3$ cm and height $10$ cm with a cone of radius $3$ cm and height $4$ cm on top. Find its volume in cm³. Use $\pi = 3.14$.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** Cylinder $= 3.14 \times 9 \times 10 = 282.6$ cm³; cone $= \dfrac13 \times 3.14 \times 9 \times 4 = 37.68$ cm³.

**Step 2.** Volume $= 282.6 + 37.68 = 320.28$ cm³.

questions.stem_md: A hemispherical steel bowl has an inner radius of $10.5$ cm. Find its capacity in cm³. Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** $V = \dfrac23\pi r^3$, with $10.5^3 = 1157.625$.

**Step 2.** $\dfrac23 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 1157.625 = 2425.5$ cm³ (about $2.43$ litres).

questions.stem_md: The hemispherical dome of a gurdwara in Amritsar has radius $7$ m. Find the cost (in ₹) of gilding its curved surface at ₹$20$ per m². Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** Curved surface $= 2\pi r^2 = 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 49 = 308$ m².

**Step 2.** Cost $= 308 \times 20 = $ ₹$6160$.

questions.stem_md: A grain silo near Karnal is a cylinder of radius $2.1$ m and height $5$ m with a conical top of height $1.5$ m. Find its volume in m³. Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.
A toy is a cone of radius $5$ cm and height $12$ cm mounted on a hemisphere of radius $5$ cm. Find its total surface area in cm². Use $\pi = 3.14$.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** $l = \sqrt{25 + 144} = 13$ cm.

**Step 2.** Surface $= \pi rl + 2\pi r^2 = 3.14 \times 5 \times (13 + 10) = 15.7 \times 23 = 361.1$ cm².

questions.stem_md: From a solid wooden cylinder of radius $3.5$ cm and height $6$ cm, a cone of the same radius and height is carved out. Find the volume of wood left in cm³. Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** Cylinder $= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 12.25 \times 6 = 231$ cm³.

**Step 2.** Wood left $= \dfrac23 \times 231 = 154$ cm³ (the cone takes one-third).

questions.stem_md: An ice-cream cone has radius $3.5$ cm and height $9$ cm. It is filled with ice cream, with a hemisphere of ice cream on top. Find the volume of ice cream. Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

answer.model_answer_md:

Cone $= \dfrac13 \times 38.5 \times 9 = 115.5$ cm³; hemisphere $= \dfrac23 \times 38.5 \times 3.5 \approx 89.83$ cm³.

answer.model_answer_md:

Separately: $2 \times 3\pi r^2 = 6\pi r^2 = 6 \times 38.5 = 231$ cm². Joined, they form a sphere: $4\pi r^2 = 154$ cm².

Saving $= 231 - 154 = 77$ cm² (the two hidden flat faces, $2\pi r^2$).

questions.solution_md: Joining hides the two flat circles.

questions.stem_md: A steel vessel is a cylinder of radius $7$ cm with a hemispherical bottom of the same radius. Its total height is $20$ cm. Find its capacity in litres. Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.solution_md: The total height includes the radius of the hemisphere.

questions.stem_md: Neha writes the total surface area of a solid made of a hemisphere and a cone of the same radius $r$ (slant height $l$) as $\pi rl + 3\pi r^2$. Find her error. Then find the correct surface area for $r = 14$ cm and $l = 50$ cm. Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

She used the hemisphere's **total** surface $3\pi r^2$, which includes its flat face. That face is glued to the cone's base and is hidden. Correct: $\pi rl + 2\pi r^2$.

questions.stem_md: The largest possible cone is cut from a solid cube of edge $6$ cm (its base touches four edges of the bottom face and its apex is at the centre of the top face). Find the volume of the cone and the percentage of the cube it uses. Use $\pi = 3.14$.

answer.model_answer_md:
The base circle fits in a $6 \times 6$ face, so $r = 3$ cm; the height is the edge, $h = 6$ cm.

An ice-cream maker in Pune compares two cup designs that hold the **same** volume.
Design A: a cone of radius $3$ cm and height $4$ cm filled, with a hemisphere of ice cream of radius $3$ cm on top.
Design B: an open cylindrical cup of radius $3$ cm, filled level to the top.

(a) Find the volume of design A in terms of $\pi$.

(b) Find the height of the cup in design B.

(c) Find the area of wrapper needed for each design (A: cone and hemisphere surfaces; B: the curved side and the bottom of the cup).

(d) Which design needs less wrapper, and by how much? Use $\pi = 3.14$.

answer.model_answer_md:

answer.model_answer_md:
Volume of the cone $= \dfrac13\pi r^2h = \dfrac13 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 7 \times 10 = \dfrac{1540}{3} \approx 513.33$ cm³.

Volume of the hemisphere $= \dfrac23\pi r^3 = \dfrac23 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 7 \times 7 = \dfrac{2156}{3} \approx 718.67$ cm³.

A storage tank is a cylinder of radius $2.1$ m and height $3$ m with a hemispherical dome of the same radius on top. Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

(a) Find the volume of the cylindrical part.

(b) Find the volume of the dome.

(c) Find the capacity of the tank in litres.

(d) Find the curved surface area of the cylindrical part and of the dome.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Cylinder: $\pi r^2h = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 2.1 \times 2.1 \times 3 = 13.86 \times 3 = 41.58$ m³.

(b) Dome: $\dfrac23\pi r^3 = \dfrac23 \times 13.86 \times 2.1 = 19.404$ m³.

(c) Capacity $= 41.58 + 19.404 = 60.984$ m³ $= 60.984 \times 1000 = 60984$ litres.

(d) Curved surface of the cylinder $= 2\pi rh = 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 2.1 \times 3 = 39.6$ m². Curved surface of the dome $= 2\pi r^2 = 2 \times 13.86 = 27.72$ m².
